opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the connection is more direct than people might assume, even though on the surface one looks like a pure science project and the other looks like a company.

The lottery ticket work started from a really simple question: if we can prune most of the weights out of a neural network after training and it still works just as well, why do we need all those weights in the first place? Could we have trained the small network from the start? What we found was that, yes, there are these sparse subnetworks hiding inside the big one that can train on their own to full accuracy, if you can find them. But the catch, and it's a big catch, is that finding them required training the full network first, often several times over. So scientifically it was exciting, but practically it didn't save anyone a dime.

And that's what stuck with me. The lottery ticket hypothesis was really telling us that the way we train neural networks is wildly inefficient. There's a lot of waste baked into the standard recipe. Pruning just happened to be the lens I used to see that, but it's not the only lever. Once you start looking, you realize there's inefficiency everywhere: in the optimizer, the data pipeline, the learning rate schedule, the architecture, how you use the hardware. Lots of small things that individually might buy you ten or twenty percent, and they compound.

So Mosaic is, in a sense, the engineering answer to the scientific question I was asking in grad school. Instead of searching for one magic sparse subnetwork, we said, let's take a systems view and attack all of those inefficiencies together, rigorously, and make training dramatically cheaper for real people training real models. The goal is the same one I had with lottery tickets: make it so you don't need Google-scale resources to build something good.

There's also a methodological connection I care about a lot. The lottery ticket work taught me to be extremely careful about empirical claims: running lots of seeds, checking baselines properly, being skeptical of results that look too good. The efficiency literature is full of methods that look great in a paper and don't hold up when you combine them with a strong baseline. A lot of what we do at Mosaic is that same scientific skepticism applied to speedup methods: does this actually make training faster at the same quality, or does it just look that way on a weak setup?

So I don't really see it as leaving research for industry. It's the same question, just with a much bigger toolbox and much higher stakes about getting the answer right.

r001.rationale: The response says the lottery ticket work exposed inefficiency in neural network training and describes Mosaic as the engineering answer to that same efficiency question.

r002.rationale: It frames Mosaic as continuing the lottery ticket inquiry while moving beyond pruning: pruning was only a lens, and Mosaic takes a systems view of other training inefficiencies.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the connection is actually pretty direct, even if it doesn't look that way on the surface. The lottery ticket hypothesis was really a question about efficiency. It was asking: these networks we train are enormously overparameterized, and yet there are these small subnetworks inside them that, if you'd found them at the start, could have trained to the same accuracy. So what does that tell us about how training works? And the practical hope was always, can we exploit that to make training cheaper?

And the honest answer from that research program was: not easily. We found that you can't just identify the winning ticket at initialization and train it from scratch, at least not at scale. You have to get a little bit into training first, and the pruning itself is expensive, so the savings mostly evaporate. That was a somewhat humbling result for me, because I'd gotten into this wanting to make training more efficient, and the specific mechanism I'd been studying turned out not to be the lever.

But the goal didn't go away. What I took from that work was that there are a lot of degrees of freedom in how you train a neural network that the field hadn't really explored systematically, because everyone was focused on architectures and datasets. The training recipe itself, the schedules, the regularization, the data ordering, the mixed precision choices, all of that was kind of folklore. And the lottery ticket result was one window into the fact that training is much weirder and has much more slack in it than we assumed.

So when Naveen and Hanlin and I started Mosaic, the premise was basically: let's stop trying to find one clever trick and instead treat efficient training as an empirical science. Let's measure every intervention rigorously, figure out which ones actually compose with each other, and build the infrastructure so that normal people can get those gains without a PhD in tuning. It's the same question I was asking in grad school, how do you get the same model for less compute, just approached from the engineering side rather than from the side of understanding why the network does what it does.

And I'd say the lottery ticket work also gave me a healthy skepticism, which turned out to be really useful at a company. I spent a lot of time in that research on things that looked great on small models and fell apart at scale. So one of the first rules at Mosaic was: nothing counts until it works on a real workload at a real size. A lot of the efficiency literature doesn't survive that test, and knowing that going in saved us a lot of time.

r001.rationale: It says the lottery ticket work aimed to make training more efficient, that the goal persisted, and Mosaic asks how to get the same model for less compute.

r002.rationale: It describes Mosaic as pursuing the same efficiency question through empirical science and engineering, but does not characterize it as the lottery ticket work continued with pruning removed.

astra-6.text:
The connection for me is really about making neural networks more efficient. With the lottery ticket hypothesis, the question was: you train this big network, but is there a much smaller network inside it that could have learned just as well? And if there is, could we somehow find it earlier and avoid doing all that extra work?

Mosaic comes at that broader goal from a more practical direction: how do we make training faster and cheaper? Sparsity is one possible approach, but you can also change the training recipe, improve how you use the hardware, or combine several smaller improvements.

So I see a pretty consistent motivation between the two. The lottery ticket work was about understanding an opportunity for efficiency. Mosaic is about turning opportunities for efficiency into something people can actually use. And there’s a real gap between those things—having fewer parameters or doing fewer operations doesn’t automatically mean your training run finishes sooner.

r001.rationale: It says both efforts share a motivation to improve neural network efficiency, describing lottery tickets as understanding efficiency opportunities and Mosaic as making them usable.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize Mosaic as the lottery ticket work with pruning removed; it presents Mosaic as a broader practical effort that may include sparsity alongside other improvements.

sol-6.1.text:
The connection for me is really about making neural network training more efficient. With the lottery ticket hypothesis, we were asking whether these big networks contain much smaller subnetworks that can train successfully on their own. That suggests there’s a lot of room to rethink how much computation we actually need.

At Mosaic, the question is broader and much more practical: how do you get to a model of a given quality with less time and less money? Sparsity might be one way to do that, but so might changing the training recipe or making better use of the hardware.

And there’s a gap between those two things. Finding a small network doesn’t automatically mean you’ve made training faster—you have to account for the cost of finding it, and whether the hardware can take advantage of it. So I see Mosaic as pursuing the same underlying motivation, but with the constraint that the efficiency has to show up in an actual training run.

r001.rationale: It links the lottery ticket work and Mosaic through the shared goal of making neural network training more efficient.

r002.rationale: It describes Mosaic as a broader practical pursuit that may use sparsity or other methods; it does not characterize Mosaic as continuing the work with pruning removed.
